text: You get a string s. Cut it into pieces so that every piece is a palindrome. Return all the ways to do that.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the pieces must cover the whole string, in order, with no gaps and no overlap. And every single piece has to read the same both ways. Is that right?
Yes. You can return the partitions in any order.
Got it. Are there any constraints on the input size?
The length is between one and sixteen, and only lowercase English letters.

Okay. Sixteen is tiny, and the question asks for all partitions, so the output itself can be exponential — an exponential search is expected. A string of length n has n minus one gaps, and each gap is a cut or not, so there are at most two to the n minus one ways to cut. The palindrome rule only removes some of them. Quick check on the example, a a b. A, a, b works. A a, b works. A, a b fails, because a b isn't a palindrome, and the whole string fails too. So the answer is those two partitions. And a single a gives just one.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would list all two to the n minus one cut patterns, build every piece, and then throw away the patterns with a bad piece. That works, but it builds lots of pieces for patterns that were dead from the first cut. This problem reminds me of backtracking over a start index — choose a piece, recurse on the rest, undo. I choose the first piece, then solve the rest of the string the same way. If the first piece isn't a palindrome, I never go deeper on it, so I only grow partitions that are still valid.

Here's the plan. One: when start reaches the end, the whole string is covered, so save a copy of path. Two: try every end from start onward; if that piece isn't a palindrome, skip to the next end. Three: push the piece, recurse from end plus one, then pop. One thing worth flagging — when a piece isn't a palindrome, I must skip it, not stop. That's continue, not break. In a b a, a b is not a palindrome, but the longer a b a is. With break, I'd return only a, b, a. That bug still passes every all-same-letter input, so I'd test a b a on purpose. There's a trade-off: a palindrome table makes each check constant time but costs n squared space. I'll start with a two-pointer check. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The search pushes a piece when it's a palindrome, recurses from end plus one, and pops on the way back; when start reaches the end, it saves path. Skip, don't stop, is built in: if the check fails, the if body just doesn't run, and the loop moves on. One thing worth flagging — substr takes a length, not an end index, which is why I compute L as end minus start plus one. With substr of start and end, the string a would give one empty piece. And the pop back is a correctness rule: without it, a a gives a, a and then a, a, a a.

Let's dry-run the code with a a b. Expected: a, a, b and a a, b. The key moment is back at the top call: after the first branch finishes, it pops a, so path is empty again. Then it tries a longer first piece, a a — a palindrome, so a whole new branch starts, ending in a a, b. Six search calls, seven palindrome checks, two answers, in the expected order. Corner cases: a gives one piece. A b c gives just one answer. A a a gives four — every cut pattern works. And a b a includes the whole string, because the loop keeps going after a b fails.

Let me think about complexity here. The worst case is every letter the same, like sixteen a's. Then every one of the two to the n minus one cut patterns is an answer: thirty-two thousand seven hundred sixty-eight partitions from sixty-five thousand five hundred thirty-six search calls. Each answer holds all n letters, so the output alone is about half a million characters. Time is n times two to the n: up to two to the n calls, each doing linear work to check and copy pieces. I can't beat the output size, so this is close to the best possible. Space is linear extra, not counting the output — the recursion stack plus path.
Look at the signature of is palindrome. Anything there?

Yes, good catch. It takes the string by value, so every check copies the whole string. On sixteen a's, that's sixty-five thousand five hundred thirty-five checks and about a million bytes copied, just to read two letters at a time. The fix is small: pass a const reference. Measured, that's fourteen point seven eight milliseconds down to four point two seven — about three and a half times faster, with no change to the logic. Oh, one more thing — the usual follow-up is the palindrome table. At n equals sixteen it gave no gain, four point six three milliseconds, because the time goes into building the output, not into the checks. So I'd ship the const reference fix first, and only add the table if a profile says so.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You explained why it's skip and not stop, with a b a, where a b fails but a b a works, and you noted a break bug would still pass all-same-letter tests. You tied the complexity to the output size. And on the optimization, you backed it with numbers for the const reference, and you were honest that the table didn't help here. Good work.
